question: How does the Muslim belief about the Prophet ﷺ differ from the Christian belief about Jesus?
asked: Someone in my office said to me: your version of Muhammad ﷺ is like our version of Jesus. You have to believe in Muhammad ﷺ to be saved; we believe in Jesus to be saved. You have to go through Muhammad ﷺ to get to your God; we go through Jesus to get to God the Father. You believe in the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ, and we too believe in Jesus interceding for us. What is the difference? It's the same thing. How do I explain this to my non-Muslim colleague?
answer:
The response is that the difference between their version of Isa and our Prophet ﷺ is the difference between God and man. There is no similarity whatsoever.

We believe that the Prophet ﷺ is separate and distinct from Allah. They believe that Jesus is God and God is Jesus. Their theology is that in the Trinity, each one of them is equally co-existent as God. Each one of them is eternal. Each one of them, they have all powers. They are not three separate entities: God the Father is God the Son, is the Holy Spirit.

So for us, the Prophet ﷺ is created, not the creator. For them, Jesus is the creator. And of course, they say he has a divine nature and a created nature. For us, the Prophet ﷺ is mortal, and Allah is eternal and immortal. And for them, Jesus is immortal as well. For us, the Prophet ﷺ is not all-powerful; it is Allah who is. And for them, Jesus is in fact all-powerful.

The main point, psychologically, theologically: every blessing that our Prophet ﷺ has, it is gifted to him by Allah. He did not acquire it himself. Every blessing that he has, Allah gave it to him. Whereas the Christian version of theology is that Jesus has that internally, inherently. No one else gifted it to him; he himself is all-powerful and all-knowledgeable.

So we believe every fadilah, every fadl, every merit that our Prophet ﷺ has, the English word is: it is contingent. It means it is upon Allah to give it and then to execute it. Otherwise, the Prophet ﷺ himself is not the Khaliq. He doesn't say "kun fayakun."

And therefore, **the shafa'ah of the Prophet ﷺ is conditional, not unconditional.** This is a very important point. The shafa'ah of the Prophet ﷺ is conditional. It means he has the right to ask; it is up to Allah to accept or to not accept. And this is very explicit. There is no makhluq that has the right to demand something from Allah and Allah must give it to him. Otherwise, if there were such a makhluq, that makhluq becomes the Rabb, a'udhu billah. Impossible.

And that's why Allah says in the Qur'an: all shafa'ah belongs to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. As Allah says in the Qur'an: no one can intercede except for whom Allah is pleased with. And in Ayat al-Kursi, what is the phrase in Ayat al-Kursi? See, here is the point.

And we learn in the hadith of Sahih Bukhari that the Prophet ﷺ will say that he will prostrate in front of the Throne. Then Allah 'azza wa jall will say... so Allah will give him permission: "Make your shafa'ah." Then, and this hadith is in Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah will demarcate for me a group of people, and Allah will say, 'Make shafa'ah for them.' So I will make shafa'ah for them." Then Allah will accept the shafa'ah. Who chose this group? Allah.

So what then is the point of the Prophet's ﷺ shafa'ah? It is an honor. It is an honor to him. Allah 'azza wa jall is showing how much He loves the Prophet ﷺ. But at the end of the day, the Prophet ﷺ, even if and though he is afdal al-makhluqat and akram al-makhluqat and Sayyid al-Anbiya' wal-Mursalin, still he does not have the unconditional right to demand.

The hadith is in Sahih Bukhari as well: when Abu Talib died, the Prophet ﷺ said, "I will continue to ask Allah to forgive you until Allah stops me." So he made shafa'ah for his uncle Abu Talib, and Allah 'azza wa jall revealed in the Qur'an three verses about this. Of them: it is not befitting for the Prophet ﷺ and the believers to ask Allah to forgive the pagans, even if they are your relatives, after it has been told to you that the mushrikeen are going to Jahannam.

And Allah says in the Qur'an: there is a good example for you in Ibrahim. There is one thing Ibrahim did that, Ya Rasulallah, you should not follow him in. This is in the Qur'an: one thing, Ya Rasulallah, don't follow Ibrahim in. One thing; what is it? When Ibrahim said to his father, "I will ask Allah to forgive you."

So Allah says Ibrahim is a role model to you, Ya Rasulallah. By the way, no one in the Qur'an has been made a role model to our Nabi ﷺ other than his father Ibrahim. And Allah made one exception: follow Ibrahim in everything except one thing. And He mentions it in the Qur'an: when Ibrahim said to his father, "I will ask Allah to forgive you." Ya Rasulallah, don't follow him in that.

So from all of this we learn: the difference between the conception that they have of Isa and our conception of the Prophet ﷺ is the difference between the Khaliq and the makhluq. There is no similarity whatsoever.
